analysis.one_liner: Exempts most over-the-counter derivatives and swaps from federal regulation and oversight.
analysis.headline: The bill sat in four committees for three weeks and died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, without ever getting a vote — but an essentially identical derivatives bill became law a week after it was introduced.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the commodity and derivatives laws to take most over-the-counter derivatives — the privately negotiated bets between big banks and trading companies — out from under the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. It gives swaps legal enforceability, shields bank products from that agency, lightens the rules for futures exchanges, and preempts some state securities laws. Its stated purposes include 'streamlining and eliminating unnecessary regulation' for derivatives markets.
analysis.who_benefits: Large financial institutions that deal in swaps and over-the-counter derivatives. The bill declares that contracts between 'eligible contract participants' — banks, insurance companies, hedge funds, corporations with more than $100 million in assets, and individuals with more than $10 million — are legally enforceable and exempt from the Commodity Exchange Act. Banks get their products excluded from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. Exchanges get lighter 'core principles' regulation instead of detailed rules, new authority to trade exempt commodities, and the right to let customers keep their margin money unsegregated.

how_it_helps.text: The bill exempts from the Commodity Exchange Act any derivative transaction in interest rates, currencies, securities, credit risk, and other financial indexes entered into between 'eligible contract participants' and not traded on an exchange.
It amends the securities laws to give swap agreements 'legal certainty' — making them enforceable in court without an overlay of securities or commodities regulation.
Title IV excludes identified banking products, including covered swap agreements, from Commodity Futures Trading Commission coverage.
It replaces detailed exchange regulation with 'core principles' that exchanges have 'reasonable discretion' in how they meet, and lets exchanges elect a lighter registration status.
It preempts state law for security futures products and calls for streamlined regulation of the markets and intermediaries that trade them.

analysis.who_pays: Nobody named on the face of the bill. The cost is indirect: a market measured in tens of trillions of dollars would operate with essentially no regulator watching positions, clearing, or manipulation. The bill defers the question of protecting retail customers from swaps to a study, and the public would bear the losses if the unregulated market destabilized the financial system.

drawbacks.text: The only federal oversight that remains for most exempt derivatives is limited anti-fraud and anti-manipulation provisions; no regulator would track the positions or the buildup of risk across the unregulated market.
Consumer protections for people who are not 'eligible contract participants' are put off to a study and a report to Congress rather than written into law.
The bill's own stated purposes include streamlining regulation and transforming the Commodity Futures Trading Commission into an oversight body — a reduced role the agency itself had resisted.

A fair point in the bill's favor: it does extend Commodity Futures Trading Commission jurisdiction over retail foreign-currency fraud ('bucket shops') previously left in a regulatory gap, and it includes special procedures to facilitate hedging by agricultural producers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The deal being offered is legal certainty and lower compliance costs for the largest derivatives dealers in exchange for a largely unwatched market. The bill is candid about the trade: only counterparties with $100 million in assets — or $10 million for individuals — qualify for the exemptions, so sophisticated parties get freedom while everyone outside the deal bears whatever risk the market accumulates. History has judged this trade harshly: this is the legislative template under which energy derivatives went unregulated (the period of the Enron energy-market manipulations) and in which the credit-default-swap market grew unchecked ahead of the 2008 crisis, when taxpayers spent hundreds of billions stabilizing institutions that had sold such swaps. The bill does close a genuine retail-forex fraud gap, but that is a small provision beside the scale of what it removes from oversight.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the last weeks of a dying Congress, sent to four committees, and expired with the Congress in January 2001 — but a nearly identical version passed and was signed into law that same month.

narrative.text: Rep. Thomas Ewing introduced the bill on December 14, 2000, with four cosponsors — three Republicans and one Democrat — and introductory remarks were printed in the Congressional Record.
The same day, it was referred to four committees — Agriculture, Banking and Financial Services, Commerce, and Judiciary — and to a Finance and Hazardous Materials subcommittee.
No committee or floor action was ever recorded; the bill died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

The Commodity Futures Modernization Act of 2000 — a bill with the same short title and the same deregulatory structure covering over-the-counter derivatives, swaps, and bank products — was enacted into law in late December 2000 through a different vehicle, so the substance of this bill became law despite this bill never moving.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people gained nothing when this bill died, because an essentially identical derivatives deregulation was enacted into law through another vehicle in the same month. The winners were the large banks and trading companies whose over-the-counter derivative and swap business was exempted from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission — the deal that later produced the Enron energy-derivatives loophole and an unregulated credit-default-swap market that helped crash the financial system in 2008.

against.what_they_did: Pressed the position that over-the-counter derivatives between sophisticated dealers should stay outside the Commodity Futures Trading Commission's authority, the approach this bill embodies.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and four cosponsors split 4 Republicans to 1 Democrat, and the parallel derivatives legislation that did become law that month passed with broad bipartisan support.

industries.industry: Over-the-counter derivatives dealers and investment banks
industries.note: The bill makes their privately negotiated derivative and swap contracts legally enforceable while removing them from the Commodity Exchange Act, leaving only narrow anti-fraud provisions. Their gain — an unwatched market — is precisely the systemic risk the public bears.
Title IV excludes identified banking products and covered swap agreements from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, ending jurisdictional fights over who regulates bank derivatives.

The exemption covers commodity swaps, weather derivatives, and other over-the-counter energy instruments traded between large counterparties, the market in which later energy-price manipulation occurred with no federal regulator watching.

industries.industry: Futures exchanges and electronic trading facilities
industries.note: Exchanges get lighter 'core principles' regulation with discretion over compliance, new authority to trade exempt commodities, and permission to let eligible customers keep margin funds unsegregated. Some of this (cheaper hedging) does serve end users like farmers and airlines.
The bill includes special procedures to encourage and facilitate bona fide hedging by agricultural producers, letting farmers lock in prices more easily.
The bill preempts state law for security futures products, taking state-level investor protections off the books.
